DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
The proposal may well be worth doing: the hotel does look underpriced against its set. But the evidence and revenue figures don't support the confidence in the description. The headline number is calculated on the wrong room count, the "direct test" of price sensitivity is confounded by seasonality, and the two-night minimum clashes with the paper's own data on wedding guests.

## Major issues

**1. The revenue estimate uses 124 rooms; the hotel has 112.**
Section 2 says Harbourside has 112 rooms, but Section 5 calculates "across our 124 rooms."
- With 124 rooms: 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£204,000**
- With 112 rooms: 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**

The headline figure is about £20,000 too high before any other adjustment.

**2. The estimate assumes every occupied weekend room pays BAR.**
The £20 rise applies only to rooms sold at Best Available Rate, but the calculation applies it to all occupied weekend rooms. The paper itself identifies business that won't pay the new BAR:
- **Wedding blocks** make up about 38% of Saturday-night bookings, booked through the couple and probably at a negotiated rate.
- **Contracted corporate and group rates** are explicitly honoured.
- **OTA bookings** pay commission, typically 15–20%, so the hotel keeps only part of each £20.

If, say, a third of weekend rooms are on non-BAR rates and a share of the remainder comes through OTAs, the realistic gain at current occupancy is closer to **£110,000–£130,000**. The paper should state the BAR share of weekend room nights from its booking data and use that.

**3. The June-to-July "test" mostly reflects seasonality, not price.**
The £10 rise took effect in the last week of June, and July occupancy rose from 81% to 89%. But Section 2 explains that July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays, and August reached 93% under the same rate. July would have been well above June in any case. To isolate the price effect, the paper would need to compare July 2025 with July 2024, or ideally the months after the rise with the same months a year earlier, adjusting for any market-wide trend.

So the data are consistent with no price sensitivity. They are equally consistent with substantial sensitivity hidden by a seasonal surge. They can't support "our weekend guests are not price sensitive," and certainly not the suggestion that higher rates *raised* demand.

**4. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business.**
Section 4 says wedding guests, about 38% of Saturday bookings, typically arrive Saturday and leave Sunday. A two-night minimum on any stay including Saturday would either force them to pay for a night they don't want or push them to other hotels. Weddings are booked many months ahead, so couples planning 2027 weddings may move their room blocks, or recommend other hotels, well before any monthly monitoring would show it.

The minimum is also likely to cost revenue on the roughly 21 Saturdays that didn't sell out in 2025. On those nights, a one-night Saturday booking is pure gain, and refusing it leaves rooms empty.

The author describes the unquantified minimum-stay effect as upside that makes £204,000 a "floor." Its net effect could just as easily be negative. A more targeted approach would apply the minimum only on dates forecast to sell out, exclude wedding blocks, or price the restriction through a premium on one-night Saturday stays rather than banning them.

**5. Assuming occupancy holds isn't "prudent."**
Section 5 calls the assumption that occupancy is maintained "prudent," and the description calls it conservative. It's actually the optimistic case for a 14% price rise. A prudent estimate would model a range of outcomes. A break-even calculation gives a useful anchor:
- Current revenue per available weekend room: £145 × 79% ≈ £114.55
- At £165, occupancy can fall to about **69%**, roughly 10 points, before room revenue drops below today's.

That's a reasonable margin of safety, and stating it would be more persuasive than claiming occupancy won't move.

## Smaller issues

- **Value-for-money scores will fall with price.** The 8.4 score was earned at £145, and a higher price will lower it. It suggests there is room to raise rates, but it doesn't show guests won't respond to the rise.
- **The monitoring trigger.** Comparing each month with the same month in 2025 is the right approach. "Review the rate" needs a defined action, though. Monthly occupancy also lags forward bookings, so weekly pace for future weekends would give earlier warning than results "within a month."
- **The "floor" language.** Section 7 says the changes will deliver "at least £204,000." Given points 1–4, that should be rewritten as an estimate with stated assumptions.
- **First-year phasing.** Stays from 1 June will include bookings already made at £145, and the first year has only seven months under the new rate. The 2026 gain will be well below the annual figure.
- **Competitor positioning.** At £165 the hotel would match the cheapest competitor, at the bottom of the £165–£180 range. That's reasonable, but it is no longer "£20 to £35 below."

## What holds up

- The 2025 monthly occupancies average 79%, as stated.
- The competitor gap of £20–£35 below a £165–£180 range is correct.
- Saturday capacity is constrained, with 31 sell-outs, so there is a real case for stronger Saturday pricing.
- Protecting existing corporate and group contracts, and monitoring against the same period last year, is the right approach.

## Suggested revisions

1. Recalculate on 112 rooms and only the BAR share of weekend nights, net of OTA commission.
2. Replace the June–July comparison with a year-on-year comparison, or describe it honestly as inconclusive.
3. Add a break-even occupancy (about 69%) and a range of outcomes instead of a single "floor."
4. Rework the minimum stay: apply it only to forecast sell-out Saturdays, exclude wedding blocks, or use a price premium instead.
5. Track forward booking pace weekly, and define in advance what happens if a trigger is hit.

In short: a rate rise to £165 is defensible on competitor positioning and the break-even margin. But the paper's claim to be well evidenced rests on a miscounted room base, a seasonal coincidence and an untested minimum-stay rule that could damage the wedding business. Correcting those would give the owners a smaller but more credible figure, likely around £110,000–£130,000 a year before any minimum-stay effect.
